sanskrit.deva:
भृगुर्वै वारुणिः ।
वरुणं पितरमुपससार ।
अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्मेति ।
तस्मा एतत्प्रोवाच ।
अन्नं प्राणं चक्षुः श्रोत्रं मनो वाचमिति ।
तं होवाच ।
यतो वा इमानि भूतानि जायन्ते ।
येन जातानि जीवन्ति ।
यत्प्रयन्त्यभिसंविशन्ति ।
तद्विजिज्ञासस्व ।
तद्ब्रह्मेति ।
स तपोऽतप्यत ।
स तपस्तप्त्वा ॥ १ ॥

padaccheda.deva: भृगुः वै वारुणिः वरुणम् पितरम् उपससार अधीहि भगवः ब्रह्म इति तस्मै एतत् प्रोवाच अन्नम् प्राणम् चक्षुः श्रोत्रम् मनः वाचम् इति तम् ह उवाच यतः वै इमानि भूतानि जायन्ते येन जातानि जीवन्ति यत् प्रयन्ति अभिसंविशन्ति तत् विजिज्ञासस्व तत् ब्रह्म इति सः तपः अतप्यत सः तपः तप्त्वा

grammar.en: past passive participle n. nom. pl.

translations.text: Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, approached his father Varuṇa: ‘Revered sir, teach me Brahman.’ To him he declared this: ‘Food, prāṇa, the eye, the ear, the mind, speech.’ He said to him: ‘That from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, to which they go and into which they enter: seek to know that. That is Brahman.’ He practised austerity. Having practised austerity,

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the vallī (after the invocation saha nāv avatu): since Brahman, real, knowledge, infinite, having created the effect that begins with space and ends with the self made of food, has as it were entered into that very effect and is perceived as though possessed of distinctions, one should understand ‘I am that bliss, other than every effect, unseen and so on’; the entering is meant for this. For one who knows thus, good and bad actions do not begin another birth. This was the sense intended in the Ānandavallī, and the knowledge of Brahman is complete. From here on austerity, the means to the knowledge of Brahman, is to be taught, and the meditations on food and the rest, which have not yet been taught; so this vallī is begun.

Śaṅkara: the story is to praise the knowledge, as one taught by a father to a dear son. vai recalls a well-known person: the one known as Bhṛgu, Varuṇa's offspring. adhīhi = teach (adhyāpaya), tell. To the son who had approached in due form the father declared this: food, that is, the body; prāṇa within it, the eater; and after it the means of perception, eye, ear, mind and speech. These he named as the doors to the perception of Brahman.

Śaṅkara: having named the doors, he stated the definition of Brahman: that from which these beings, from Brahmā down to a clump of grass, are born; by which, once born, they live, keep their breath and grow; and to which at the time of destruction they go, into which they enter, becoming of one nature with it. That whose nature beings do not leave at their arising, their staying and their dissolution: this is the definition of Brahman. ‘Seek to know that Brahman in particular’: attain through food and the rest the Brahman that has this mark. Another text says: ‘those who know the prāṇa of prāṇa, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, the mind of mind, have ascertained the ancient, first Brahman’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.18), showing that these are the doors to its perception.

Śaṅkara: having heard from his father the doors to the perception of Brahman and its definition, Bhṛgu practised austerity as the means of attaining it. How did he take up austerity when it had not been taught as the means? Because what was said was incomplete. The father named food and the rest as doors and gave the definition ‘from which these beings are born’; that is incomplete, for Brahman was not pointed out directly. Otherwise he should have shown its own form to the son who wished to know: ‘this Brahman is such.’ He did not; he spoke with a remainder. So it is understood that the father surely expects another means for the knowledge of Brahman. Austerity in particular is fixed upon because it is the best of all means; it is well known in the world that for results bound to fixed means austerity is the best means. So Bhṛgu took up austerity though his father had not taught it. That austerity is the composure of the outer and inner organs, since that is the door to the attainment of Brahman: ‘the one-pointedness of the mind and of the senses is the highest austerity; it is greater than all dharmas; it is called the highest dharma’ (Mahābhārata 12.232.13).
The e-text reads yatprayanyabhisaṃviśanti; it is set right here to yat prayanty abhisaṃviśanti, as the commentary cites it.

translations.text: he understood that food is Brahman; for truly from food these beings are born, by food, once born, they live, to food they go and into it they enter. Having understood that, he again approached his father Varuṇa: ‘Revered sir, teach me Brahman.’ He said to him: ‘Seek to know Brahman by austerity. Austerity is Brahman.’ He practised austerity. Having practised austerity,

notes: Śaṅkara: he understood that food is Brahman, for food has the mark that was stated: from food these beings are born, by food they live, to food they go and into it they enter; so it is fitting that food be Brahman. Having practised austerity and understood food as Brahman by the mark and by reasoning, he fell into doubt again and approached his father. What was the cause of the doubt? That food is seen to have an origin.

Śaṅkara: austerity is taught again and again to fix it as the surpassing means: as long as the definition of Brahman is not unsurpassed and the wish to know has not ceased, so long austerity alone is your means; by austerity alone seek to know Brahman. The rest is plain. (He comments no further on the steps of prāṇa, mind and understanding, 3.3–3.5.)
The e-text reads annādadhyeva and bhutāni; they are set right here to annād dhy eva and bhūtāni.

words.meaning: in the radiance of sacred knowledge

translations.text: he understood that bliss is Brahman; for truly from bliss these beings are born, by bliss, once born, they live, to bliss they go and into it they enter. This is the knowledge of Bhṛgu and of Varuṇa, established in the highest space (of the heart). He who knows thus becomes established (in Brahman). He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great in offspring, in cattle and in the radiance of sacred knowledge, great in fame.

notes: Śaṅkara: thus, his mind purified by austerity, not seeing the definition of Brahman fulfilled in prāṇa and the rest, and entering inward step by step, Bhṛgu came by austerity alone as means to know the inmost bliss as Brahman. Therefore one who wishes to know Brahman should practise the supreme austerity, the composure of the outer and inner organs, as the means; this is the sense of the section.

Śaṅkara: now, leaving the story, the śruti states in its own words the sense the story has brought out. This knowledge, known by Bhṛgu and taught by Varuṇa, is established in the highest space, in the cave of the space of the heart, in the supreme non-dual bliss: begun from the self made of food, it is completed there. Anyone else too who by this same order, with austerity alone as means, entering in step by step, knows bliss as Brahman, becomes established in bliss, the supreme Brahman, because his knowledge is so established; that is, he becomes Brahman itself.

Śaṅkara: the seen fruit too is stated. annavān = one who has plentiful food; for if the mere having of food were meant, everyone has it, and the knowledge would make no difference. annāda = one who eats food, that is, whose digestive fire is kindled. He becomes great: by offspring, sons and the rest; by cattle, cows, horses and the like; by brahmavarcasa, the radiance that comes of quiet of mind, restraint of the senses, knowledge and the like; and great by fame, the renown that comes of good conduct.
The e-text reads ānandādhyeva; it is set right here to ānandād dhy eva.

words.meaning: in the radiance of sacred knowledge

translations.text: One should not revile food: that is the vow. Prāṇa indeed is food; the body is the eater of food. The body is established in prāṇa; prāṇa is established in the body. So this food is established in food. He who knows this food established in food becomes established. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great in offspring, in cattle and in the radiance of sacred knowledge, great in fame.

notes: Śaṅkara: moreover, since Brahman was known with food as the door, one should not revile food, as one would not a teacher: this is taught as a vow for him who knows Brahman thus. The teaching of the vow is to praise food, and food is worthy of praise as the means to the perception of Brahman.

Śaṅkara: prāṇa is food because it lies within the body; whatever is established within another is that other's food, and prāṇa is established in the body; so prāṇa is food and the body the eater. Likewise the body too is food and prāṇa the eater, because the body is established in prāṇa: the body's staying depends on prāṇa. So both of these, body and prāṇa, are food and eater: in that each is established in the other it is food; in that each is the support of the other it is the eater. He who knows this food established in food becomes established, in the very form of food and eater; and he becomes possessed of food and the rest, as before.
The e-text reads tadavratam and tadetadannmanne; they are set right here to tad vratam and tad etad annam anne.

translations.text: One should not reject food: that is the vow. Water indeed is food; light is the eater of food. Light is established in water; water is established in light. So this food is established in food. He who knows this food established in food becomes established. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great in offspring, in cattle and in the radiance of sacred knowledge, great in fame.

notes: Śaṅkara: na paricakṣīta = one should not refuse food; this is a vow as before, in praise of food. Food that is not rejected, without regard to good or bad, is thereby praised and magnified. In the same way the sense is to be construed in the sentences that follow, ‘water indeed is food’ and the rest.

translations.text: One should not turn anyone away in the matter of lodging: that is the vow. Therefore one should obtain much food by whatever means. ‘Food has been made ready for him,’ they say (to the guest). This food, made ready, (he gives) in the foremost way: in the foremost way food is made ready for him. This food, made ready, (he gives) in the middling way: in the middling way food is made ready for him. This food, made ready, (he gives) in the lowest way: in the lowest way food is made ready for him, who knows thus. (Brahman is to be meditated on) as safekeeping in speech; as gain and safekeeping in prāṇa and apāna; as action in the hands; as movement in the feet; as release in the anus: these are the human meditations. Now the divine: as satisfaction in rain; as strength in lightning; as renown in cattle; as light in the stars; as procreation, immortality and bliss in the organ of generation; as the all in space. One should meditate on that as the support: one becomes possessed of support. One should meditate on that as greatness: one becomes great. One should meditate on that as thinking: one becomes able to think. One should meditate on that as bowing: the things desired bow down to him. One should meditate on that as Brahman (the greatest): one becomes possessed of Brahman. One should meditate on that as Brahman's ‘dying around’: around him die the rivals who hate him, and around him those foes who are not dear to him. He who is here in man, and he who is yonder in the sun: he is one. He who knows thus, on departing from this world, having passed into this self made of food, having passed into this self made of prāṇa, having passed into this self made of mind, having passed into this self made of understanding, having passed into this self made of bliss, roaming through these worlds, having food at will and taking forms at will, remains singing this chant: ‘Oh! Oh! Oh! I am food, I am food, I am food! I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food! I am the maker of their union, I am the maker of their union, I am the maker of their union! I am the first-born of the true (this world), before the gods, the navel of immortality. He who gives me, he indeed thus protects me. I, food, eat him who eats food (without giving). I have overcome the whole world; (my) light is like the sun.’ (This is the fruit for him) who knows thus. Such is the secret teaching.

notes: Śaṅkara, on the vow and on the giving of food: likewise, for one who meditates on earth and space (as food and eater), the vow is not to turn away anyone who has come for lodging; and when lodging is given, food must certainly be given. Therefore one should gather much food by whatever means. Because the learned who have food say to the guest who seeks food ‘food has been made ready for him’ and do not refuse him with ‘there is none’, for that reason too one should obtain much food. The greatness of the gift of food is also stated: as and when one gives food, so and then it comes back to him. mukhataḥ = in the first age of life, or in the foremost manner, with honour: he gives the food made ready to the guest who seeks it (the sentence is to be so completed); the fruit is that food is made ready for that giver in his early age, or in the foremost manner; it comes to him as it was given. So madhyataḥ = in the middle age, or with middling courtesy; and antataḥ = in the last age, or with the lowest courtesy, with disrespect: in just that way food is made ready for him. ‘Who knows thus’: to him who knows the greatness of food as stated, and the fruit of giving it, that fruit comes.

Śaṅkara, on the meditations: now the manner of meditating on Brahman is stated. kṣema = the preserving of what has been got: Brahman is to be meditated on as established in speech in the form of safekeeping. yoga = the getting of what has not been got. Though gain and safekeeping come about while prāṇa and apāna are there, they are not caused by prāṇa and apāna alone but by Brahman; so Brahman is to be meditated on as established in prāṇa and apāna as gain and safekeeping. In the others too Brahman alone is to be meditated on as this or that: since action is brought about by Brahman, as established in the hands as action; as movement in the feet; as release in the anus. These are the mānuṣīḥ samājñāḥ: belonging to men, concerning the body; samājñā = knowledges, that is, meditations. Then the divine ones, belonging to the gods. Since rain is the cause of satisfaction through food and the rest, Brahman itself abides in rain as satisfaction; likewise as strength in lightning, as renown in cattle, as light in the stars. Procreation, immortality (the attaining of immortality through a son, by release from the debt) and ānanda, pleasure: all this, which the organ of generation occasions, is Brahman established there in that form. All is established in space; so whatever is ‘all’ in space is Brahman, and that space is Brahman; therefore one should meditate on it as the support of all.

Śaṅkara, on the fruits: by meditating on the quality of support one becomes possessed of support. So in the earlier ones too: whatever fruit is read there is Brahman itself, and by meditating on it one comes to possess it; another śruti says, ‘as they meditate on him, that he becomes’ (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.5.2.20). mahaḥ = possessed of the quality of greatness. manaḥ = thinking (manana); mānavān = able to think. namaḥ = bowing: possessed of the quality of bowing; the kāmāḥ, the things desired, the objects of enjoyment, bow down to the meditator. brahma = the greatest (parivṛḍhatama); brahmavān = he comes to have that quality. brahmaṇaḥ parimaraḥ: that in which the five deities die around, lightning, rain, the moon, the sun and fire; so the wind is the parimara, as is well known from another śruti. This same wind is not other than space; so space is the parimara of Brahman, and one should meditate on space, whose self is the wind, as the parimara of Brahman. Rivals may be hating or not hating, so they are qualified: the rivals who hate him die around him, they give up their breath; and those foes who are not dear to him, even if they do not hate him, also die.

Śaṅkara, on what the teaching of food and eater establishes: from ‘prāṇa indeed is food, the body the eater of food’ down to space, being food and eater has been stated of the effect alone. What follows from that? That transmigration, which is made by being enjoyed and enjoyer, belongs to the effect alone and not to the Self; of the Self it is spoken only figuratively, through error. Objection: the self too is an effect of the supreme Self, so transmigration fits it. No: the śruti of entering is of one who does not transmigrate. In ‘having created that, it entered that very thing’ (2.6) the entering into the effects is heard of the supreme Self, the cause of space and the rest, which does not transmigrate; so the jīva-self that has entered the effect is the supreme itself, not transmigrating. And the same agent is fitting in ‘having created, it entered’: the suffix ktvā is right only if the agent of creating and of entering is one. Objection: but the one who has entered comes to another state. No: entering was already shown (at 2.6) to have another sense. Objection: from the specific text ‘with this jīva’ (Chāndogya 6.3.2) the entering is with another property. No: ‘that thou art’ (Chāndogya 6.8.7) states its being that again. Objection: that is an imagined identification, to remove the other state from one who has come into it. No: because of the co-reference in ‘that is the true, that is the Self, that thou art’. Objection: the transmigration of the jīva is seen. No: the perceiver cannot be perceived. Objection: the self qualified by the properties of transmigration is perceived. No: properties are not separate from their bearer and so cannot be its objects, just as heat and light cannot be what is burnt and lit. Objection: from the sight of fear and the like, its being a sufferer is inferred. No: fear and the like, and pain, being perceived, are not properties of the perceiver. Objection: this conflicts with the reasoned systems of Kapila, Kaṇāda and others. No: having no root and conflicting with the Veda, they are fittingly in error. So by śruti and by reasoning it is established that the Self does not transmigrate; and from its oneness. How oneness? ‘He who is here in man, and he who is yonder in the sun: he is one’ and the rest, all as before (2.8).

Śaṅkara, on the knower's roaming and chant: the sense of the verse ‘real, knowledge, infinite’ was explained at length by the Ānandavallī, but not the sense of its statement of the fruit, ‘he enjoys all desires, together with Brahman, the all-knowing’ (2.1): what the desires are, what their objects, and how he enjoys them together with Brahman. That is taken up now. In the story of father and son, a supplement to the earlier knowledge, austerity was taught as the means to the knowledge of Brahman; the effect from prāṇa to space was applied as food and eater; and meditations on Brahman were taught. All the desires that are won each by its own many means and have for objects the differing effects, space and the rest, have thus been shown. But in oneness there can be neither desire nor one who desires, all difference being the Self. How then does he who knows thus enjoy all desires at once in the form of Brahman? Because he is the self of all. How so? By the knowledge of the oneness of the self in man and in the sun he sets aside higher and lower, passes in order through the selves from the one made of food to the one made of bliss, which ignorance has fashioned, and reaches the fruit: Brahman, real, knowledge, infinite, unseen and so on, natural bliss, unborn, deathless, fearless, non-dual. Then he roams through these worlds, earth and the rest: kāmānnī, whose food is at his will; kāmarūpī, whose forms are at his will; roaming, that is, experiencing these worlds as himself, being the self of all. He remains singing this sāman: Brahman itself is the sāman, because it is the same (sama), not other than anything; singing = uttering, proclaiming the oneness of the Self for the good of the world, and its fruit, the utter fulfilment of all ends. hāvu means ‘oh!’, to make known extreme wonder.

Śaṅkara, on the chant: what is the wonder? Though I am the non-dual, stainless Self, I myself am food and the eater of food. And I myself am the ślokakṛt: śloka is the union of food and eater, and its maker is the conscious one; or, the maker of the aggregate of food itself, which, being manifold and for the sake of another, the eater, is put together because it is for another. The saying thrice is to declare the wonder. prathamajāḥ = the first-born of ṛta, the true, this world with form and without form, and before the gods; amṛtasya nābhiḥ = the centre of immortality: the immortality of living beings rests in me. Whoever gives me, food, to those who seek food, declaring me as food, he thus protects me unharmed, as I am. But he who, when the time has come, eats food without giving me to those who ask, him, the man eating food, I who am food eat in return.

Śaṅkara, on a doubt and the close: ‘then I am afraid of liberation, the attaining of being the self of all; let me stay in transmigration, since even when liberated I should, being food, be eaten.’ Do not fear so: the enjoying of all desires lies within the sphere of worldly dealing. The knower has by knowledge passed beyond that sphere, marked by food, eater and the rest and made by ignorance, and has reached Brahman-hood; for him there is no second thing of which he could be afraid; so liberation is not to be feared. Then why does he say ‘I am food, I am the eater of food’? This dealing marked by food and eater, an effect, is mere dealing and not a real thing; yet, being caused by Brahman and unreal apart from Brahman, it is spoken of in praise of the becoming Brahman that is the result of the knowledge of Brahman. So for one who has become Brahman there is not even a trace of fear and such faults, which come of ignorance, ignorance being cut off. bhuvanam = what beings from Brahmā down resort to, or that in which beings come to be; abhyabhavām = I overcome it by my own supreme, lordly nature. suvar na jyotiḥ: suvar is the sun and na has the sense of ‘like’: my light is like the sun, shining once for all. iti: the Upaniṣad is the knowledge of the supreme Self taught in the two vallīs; for him who, having become calm, restrained, withdrawn, forbearing and collected, and having taken up great austerity like Bhṛgu, knows this Upaniṣad as taught, there is this fruit, liberation as stated. (The commentary closes with the invocation saha nāv avatu.)
The words are given here in their ordinary form; the text has the lengthened (pluta) vowels of the chant: hā3vu, annādo3, ṛtā3sya, nā3bhāyi (= nābhiḥ), mā3vāḥ, ā3dmi, abhyabhavā3m.

The e-text of the mūla omits ya evaṃ veda after antato 'smā annaṃ rādhyate; it is supplied here from the commentary, which cites and explains it. The e-text also reads tadavratam, mukhato 'naṃ, madhyato 'naṃ, edadvai, tadabrahmetyupāsīta, tadabrahmaṇaḥ and imāṃllokan; they are set right here to tad vratam, mukhato 'nnaṃ, madhyato 'nnaṃ, etad vai, tad brahmety upāsīta, tad brahmaṇaḥ and imāṃl lokān.
